parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones a boat company to book a seal-watching trip for his family.
script: Good morning, Skerry Point Boat Trips, Megan speaking. How can I help?
Hello there. I'd like to book a seal-watching trip for my family, please. We picked up your leaflet at the tourist office yesterday, and the children haven't stopped talking about it since.
Lovely. Let me just open the booking system. Could I take a name first, please?
And could you spell the surname for me?
Of course. It's H-A-L-L-W-O-R-T-H. Most people write it with only one L in the middle, but there are two.
Got it, Hallworth. And a contact number, in case we have to cancel because of the weather?
Well, our home number is 01632 960 417, but we're staying on a campsite all week, so you'd better use my mobile. That's 07845 330 169.
07845 330 169. Thank you. Now, which day were you thinking of?
Wednesday, if possible. The forecast for Wednesday looks nice and calm.
Ah, I'm afraid Wednesday is fully booked. A school group has hired the whole boat. I do have places on Thursday, though.
Thursday would be fine. My wife says she's flexible.
Great. On Thursdays we run one trip at 9 o'clock and another at 10.30. The earlier one is better for spotting wildlife, to be honest.
Nine is a bit early with three children, though. We'd prefer 10.30, if the seals will still be there.
Oh, they will. At that time the tide is going out and they haul themselves onto the sandbank, so it's actually the best trip of the day. I'll put you down for 10.30. How many are in your group?
Two adults and three children. Jamie is twelve, Hannah is nine, and little Ollie is four.
Children under five travel free, so Ollie doesn't pay. That means 2 adults and 2 children paying.
That's fine. How much is it?
Adults are 18 pounds 50 and children are 11 pounds. That's the summer price. If your friends went in the spring, they'd have paid less, because it was 16 pounds then.
Right, 18 pounds 50 for adults. And how long does the trip last?

About two hours, there and back. Now, where you meet is important. We leave from the quay, outside the Lobster Café. Please don't go to the harbour office by mistake, because that's where the fishing trips leave from.
The Lobster Café, got it. Is there anywhere to park?
The main harbour car park is 7 pounds for the day, but there's a smaller one up by the lighthouse that only charges 5 pounds. It's a ten-minute walk down to the quay, though.
Five pounds sounds better, and the children can do with the walk. What should we bring?
It can be very breezy out on the water, even in July, so a waterproof jacket is more important than sun cream. Wear flat shoes as well, because the deck gets slippery.
And can we buy anything to eat on board?
There's a little kiosk. The coffee machine is broken at the moment, so it's just hot chocolate and biscuits. I'd bring sandwiches if I were you.
Good idea. Are dogs allowed? Ours is quite fond of the sea.
I'm afraid not, because the seals are easily frightened. But the campsite might have a kennel service.
I'll ask them. Thank you very much, Megan.
You're welcome. I'll send a confirmation text to your mobile this afternoon. See you on Thursday, Mr Hallworth.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: The coordinator of outdoor learning at a primary school talks to parents about next year's school trips.
script: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming along on such a wet night. My name's Craig Dunstan, and I'm the coordinator of outdoor learning here at Kestrel Bay Primary. I'd like to take about fifteen minutes to explain how our school trips will work this year, and then there'll be time for your questions.

First of all, why have we changed things? Some of you may think it was about money. It wasn't. We've kept the fees roughly where they were. Others may remember the parents' survey from two years ago, which showed that most families were perfectly happy with the old programme. The real reason is the new curriculum, which asks us to teach more science and geography outdoors. So every trip you'll hear about tonight is now linked to what the children are studying that term, and any trip that wasn't linked to lessons has been dropped.

Let me take you through the year groups. We start with Year 2, who will make a day trip to Carrow Castle. It's only forty minutes by coach, and it fits in with their topic on homes in the past. The children dress up, they draw the old kitchens, and, I'm told, they spend most of the day shouting down the well.

Year 3 will be going to Hollin Farm for two nights. That's their first time away from home, which is a big step for some of them. In previous years Year 3 went to the caves at Ashby, but our insurers raised the cost so much that we had to stop. The farm is a better choice anyway, because the children learn where food comes from, and they help to feed the animals before breakfast.

Year 4 will spend a day at Sandhaven, doing a beach survey. They count and measure the shells and seaweed along a marked line and compare the results with last year's class. We did think about bringing back the canal boat day for this group, but the operator retired and there's nobody to replace him.

In Year 5 the children go to Greywood Forest for three nights. They sleep in tents, they cook their own meals, and they build shelters. Parents sometimes worry about how much sleep their children will get, and I can't promise much. But the staff who go on that trip tell me that, once they're past the second night, the children manage by themselves in ways they never do at school.

And finally, Year 6 will spend four nights in a mountain hut in the Larkfell range, at the end of the summer term. It's a long walk up, so we choose the date carefully, and the weather is checked every morning. It's the most demanding trip we offer, and the one they remember longest.

A word about the overnight stays in general. Friendships do grow stronger, and the children certainly come back fitter, but those are side effects. What we really notice is independence. A child who has packed a bag, looked after his own things and got up on time for a week in the woods is a different person in the classroom.

Now to the question you're all waiting for: the cost. I want to be clear that every child can go. There isn't a single fixed price. Instead, we ask for a contribution based on your household income, in three bands. You fill in one short form, and nobody is asked to provide proof. The most any family pays for the mountain trip is 90 pounds, and the lowest band pays a fifth of that. A local charity does give us a grant, but it only covers part of the total, so the contributions are still essential.

Next, some dates. You'll find an envelope in your child's bag this week with a booking form and a medical form. I need the medical form back by the end of this month, please, because the leaders must know about allergies and medication well before we travel. You don't need to pay anything yet. The deposit isn't due until March, and I'll send a reminder.

Finally, we'd love some of you to come with us as helpers. Every trip needs more adults than we have teachers. If you'd like to help, you must have a background check before you can go, and I'd advise you to apply straight away, because it takes about three weeks. We also run a training evening in February, which is useful, but it's optional. You don't have to have led a group before. Enthusiasm and a good pair of boots are the main requirements.
Right, that's all from me. Does anyone have any questions?

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Ellie and Marcus, plan a seminar presentation on bilingual children.
script: Hi, Marcus. Sorry I'm late. Have you had a chance to look through the notes for our seminar?
Yes, I read them on the bus. Before we start, I'm really glad we chose bilingual children. It was my idea, but I'd forgotten how interesting it is.
Was it that documentary you mentioned, the one about children in Wales?

No, funnily enough. I did see it, but it wasn't that. My cousin in Auckland is raising her twins in Samoan and English, and she kept asking me whether it would confuse them. I didn't know what to say, so I thought, well, let's find out. I suppose Dr Hanley's lecture last term helped too, but that came afterwards.

Right. Well, what struck me most when I did the reading was the early research. I knew the studies were small, with a few dozen children in a handful of schools, but I didn't expect the conclusions to be so negative. Those researchers actually said that speaking two languages caused mental confusion and lowered intelligence.

Yes, and that was partly because the children they tested were poor immigrants being examined in a language they barely knew. Of course they scored badly. It's a good example of how not to design an experiment.
The next thing is the claim that bilingual people are better at switching between tasks. I'd like to say that's well established.
I'm not sure we can. A few experiments found a clear advantage, but when other teams repeated them, they found nothing. So I'd say the evidence is mixed, and we should be honest about that.
Fair enough. We'll say it's possible but not proven. Now, for the brain imaging results, I thought we could show a short video from the lab that did the scans.

Hmm. It's three minutes long, and that would eat into our time. And the table of figures is too hard to read from the back of the room. What about one simple diagram that shows which regions of the brain are more active?
Yes, that's much better. I can draw it tonight.
Great. What worries me most about the whole talk is the timing. We've got twenty minutes, and I think we've planned too much, so there'll be hardly any time left for questions.
I agree, that's the real weakness. I was going to say we haven't included the teachers' point of view, but there's no room for that anyway.
No, we can leave it. Right, let's go through the plan, section by section.
OK. The introduction. I wrote about four minutes, with the history of the subject and some definitions.
That's far too long. Everyone in the seminar group knows what bilingual means. I'd cut it to two minutes.
All right, I'll shorten it. Next is the early research. You suggested leaving that out altogether, didn't you?
Well, I wondered about it, because everybody has heard that story. But I suppose we need it as a contrast with the modern findings.
Exactly. So what if we put a one-page summary on the course website before the seminar, and ask everyone to read it beforehand? Then we only need a minute on it.
Good, that solves it. Then the case study of my cousin's family. I thought we could simply describe them.

But that's a bit dry. Couldn't you bring in some real examples, a few sentences the twins actually say, where they mix Samoan and English in the same sentence? People would understand straight away what bilingual speech is really like.
Yes, I'll ask my cousin's permission and put in some examples. Now, the group discussion. At the moment it comes at the end, just before the conclusion.
And that's when everyone is tired. I think we should swap it with the brain imaging section, so the discussion comes while people still have energy, and the brain scans come last.
Good idea. Finally, the conclusion. We're supposed to give some recommendations for teachers, but I'm not sure if Dr Hanley wants those.
I don't know either. We'd better ask her before we write it, rather than guess.
I'll email her tonight. Shall we go through the slides now?
Yes, let's start with the title slide.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about the invention of the clock and the idea of time-keeping.
script: Good morning. Today I want to look at one of the most ordinary objects in our lives, the clock, and ask a question that sounds simple: how did human beings come to divide the day into equal units, and why did they feel the need to?

Let's begin with the earliest devices. About 3,500 years ago, the Egyptians were using shadow clocks, which were upright sticks and, later, tall obelisks that cast a shadow across a scale. The idea behind the sundial is simple and it works well in a sunny country, but it has obvious weaknesses. It's no use at night, and it's not much use on cloudy days either, which in most of northern Europe means most days. So people looked for something that worked in any weather.

The answer was the water clock. Water drips from one vessel into another, and the level shows how much time has passed. Water clocks were known in Egypt and Babylon, but they were used with particular enthusiasm in Athens, where they were installed in the law courts. Each speaker in a trial was given a fixed measure of water, and when it ran out, he had to stop talking. So the clock's first job in public life was to limit the length of speeches, which many of us would welcome today.

Water clocks had a drawback, though. The flow slows down as the vessel empties, and clever engineers solved that by shaping the vessel like a cone. But the flow also depends on temperature, because cold water runs more slowly than warm, and that problem was never really solved. A water clock in a cold temple could be wrong by a considerable margin by the end of a winter morning.

Now, the mechanical clock appeared in Europe towards the end of the thirteenth century. We don't know exactly where or by whom, because nobody signed their work. What we do know is who the first customers were. It wasn't merchants or kings. It was the monasteries, where the monks had to be woken at fixed times during the night to pray, and someone had to know when to ring the bell. In fact the word clock comes from an old word for a bell, and these early machines did nothing else. They had no face at all. They simply struck the hours.

They were also remarkably inaccurate. Some writers of the time claimed that a good clock might be an hour out in a day, but modern tests on working copies suggest that the typical error was nearer 15 minutes a day. That was still enough that someone had to check the machine against a sundial every noon and put it right.

The big step forward came in 1656, when the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens, that's H-U-Y-G-E-N-S, built a clock regulated by a swinging pendulum. Galileo had studied the idea decades earlier, but he never built a working clock. Within a few years the best pendulum clocks were keeping time to within about 10 seconds a day. For the first time, minutes mattered, and clockmakers began adding a second hand.

Pendulums, however, have a problem at sea, since a ship doesn't stay still. This was serious, because accurate time is the key to navigation. Sailors could work out their latitude from the height of the sun without much difficulty. But to find longitude, they needed to know exactly what time it was at their home port, and then compare it with the local time on the ship. Without a reliable clock, ships were wrecked and thousands of sailors drowned. In 1714 the British government offered an enormous prize to anyone who could solve the problem, and it was won, after decades of effort, by a Yorkshire clockmaker called John Harrison, who built a spring-driven clock that kept time through storms.

My last example concerns the land rather than the sea. Until the nineteenth century, every town set its clocks by the sun, so noon in Bristol came about ten minutes after noon in London. This didn't matter when the fastest thing on the road was a horse. But when the railways arrived, with their timetables, it caused chaos, and in the 1840s the British railway companies began to run all their trains on London time. The idea spread. In 1884 an international conference in Washington chose Greenwich as the zero line for longitude, and that decision paved the way for the world's 24 time zones that we use today.
So the history of the clock is really a history of society's changing needs: first for ritual, then for law, navigation and trade. Next week we'll look at how the same pressures shaped the calendar.

passages.title: The Long Road to Painless Surgery
paras: A  Until the middle of the nineteenth century, a surgeon's most valuable skills were speed and strength. Operations were carried out on patients who were wide awake, held down by assistants or strapped to the table, often while students watched from the gallery. A fast surgeon could remove a leg in under a minute, because every extra second increased both the suffering and the danger that the patient would die of shock. All that could be offered beforehand was alcohol, a dose of opium or, in some hospitals, a sharp blow to the head. Many people with tumours or badly broken bones chose to live with their condition rather than face the cure, and surgery was usually reserved for cases in which the alternative was certain death.

B  People had not ignored the problem. Physicians in ancient Greece and Rome prescribed the juice of the mandrake plant, and Chinese and Arab writers described mixtures of herbs that dulled the senses. Such remedies were unreliable. The dose that sent one patient to sleep might have no effect on a second and kill a third, and no one had a way of measuring what was happening inside the body. What was lacking was not imagination but chemistry: before the eighteenth century nobody could produce a pure gas, still less predict what it might do to a living person. Progress had to wait for the scientists who learned to isolate and handle the gases of the air.

C  The first of these gases to attract attention was nitrous oxide, prepared in 1772 by the English clergyman and chemist Joseph Priestley. In 1799 a young researcher named Humphry Davy, who had been inhaling the gas to see what it did, noticed that it eased the pain of an aching tooth. He wrote that it might one day be used in operations, but nobody took the suggestion seriously. For the next forty years nitrous oxide was valued chiefly as entertainment. Travelling showmen offered 'laughing gas' to volunteers at fairs, and audiences enjoyed watching the stumbling and giggling that followed. Most surgeons regarded it as a toy.

D  The turning point came in the United States. In 1844 a dentist from Hartford, Horace Wells, watched a volunteer at one such show injure his leg without seeming to feel it. Wells had one of his own teeth pulled while breathing the gas, and felt nothing. He then arranged a public demonstration at a Boston hospital, but the patient cried out and the students in the audience jeered. Wells was humiliated. It was a former colleague, William Morton, who succeeded in 1846. Using ether, a liquid whose vapour sends the patient to sleep, Morton enabled a surgeon at Massachusetts General Hospital to remove a growth from a man's neck while he lay quietly. News crossed the Atlantic within weeks, and by December a surgeon in London was operating on a patient who felt no pain.

E  Ether had drawbacks. Its smell was unpleasant, it irritated the lungs, and it was highly flammable, a serious problem in an age of candles and gas lamps. In 1847 the Edinburgh doctor James Simpson began looking for something better. One evening he and two colleagues sat at his dining table and inhaled the vapour of several liquids; chloroform was the one that left all three on the floor. Within weeks Simpson was using it to ease childbirth. Some clergymen objected, arguing that pain in labour was part of a divine plan, but opposition faded in 1853 when Queen Victoria accepted chloroform for the birth of her eighth child. The physician who administered it, John Snow, became the first doctor to devote himself to the study of anaesthetics, working out doses with a precision that his predecessors had lacked. Chloroform nevertheless carried a risk of stopping the heart, and deaths were not uncommon.

F  The twentieth century brought a more varied toolkit. Anaesthetists no longer needed to put a patient fully to sleep for minor procedures. In 1884 an Austrian eye surgeon named Karl Koller discovered that cocaine could numb the surface of the eye, and safer synthetic substances for use on a small area followed early in the next century. Drugs derived from curare, once used on the arrowheads of South American hunters, were introduced in the 1940s; by relaxing the muscles they allowed surgeons to operate with far lighter doses of anaesthetic. Monitors that track the heartbeat, blood pressure and oxygen levels turned the work of the anaesthetist from an art into a science.

G  Today, for a healthy patient, the chance of dying from the anaesthetic itself is remote, far smaller than the risks of the operation and tiny compared with the dangers of a century ago. Yet one puzzle remains unsolved. Researchers can describe in detail what anaesthetics do to individual nerve cells, but exactly how a drug, whether a gas or an injection, switches off consciousness altogether is still debated. The question is of more than theoretical interest. A small number of patients wake during surgery, and a better understanding of the mechanism might prevent that from happening.

passages.title: Counting without Numbers
paras: A  To anyone raised on a language such as English, counting seems as natural as walking. Yet linguists have documented a dozen or so languages whose number vocabulary stops at two or three words, and a larger group in which the numbers above ten have been borrowed from outsiders. The Ikuru, a community of about four hundred hunter-gatherers living along a tributary of the Amazon, have words that translate roughly as 'one', 'two' and 'many'. Their neighbours, who trade with riverboat merchants, have counting systems that reach into the hundreds. The contrast raises an old question: do people count because they have number words, or do they invent number words because they need to count?

B  The most careful investigation of the Ikuru was carried out by the psychologist Ilse Marchetti, who spent three field seasons in the community. In one series of tests, she placed a row of seven nuts on a mat and asked participants to lay out the same number of balloons beside them. They did so without difficulty, pairing each nut with a balloon. But when the nuts were hidden under a cloth and the participants had to reproduce the quantity from memory, accuracy fell sharply for any number above three. The Ikuru were no less intelligent than the city students who took the same tests; they simply had no tool for holding an exact quantity in mind.

C  Marchetti noticed that the Ikuru rarely needed such a tool. Food is shared according to kinship rather than quantity, nobody owns livestock or stores grain, and debts are remembered as favours rather than sums. A hunter returning with 'many' fish has no reason to say whether there were twelve or fourteen. Where people do have something to count, the picture changes. Among farming communities, herd size, plot boundaries, taxes and trade all encourage precision, and number words multiply. Counting, in this view, is less like a sense that we are born with than like a technology, adopted when its usefulness outweighs the effort of learning it.

D  Technologies, however, can take surprising forms. In the highlands of New Guinea, the Dauri people count on their bodies, touching a sequence of twenty-seven points that runs from the thumb up the arm to the nose and down the other side. The word for each point doubles as the word for a number, so that a trader can show a price by touching his own shoulder. Archaeologists have also found notched bones, many thousands of years old, which suggest that tallying, the recording of quantity with no words at all, may be older than number language. People, it seems, can store quantity in objects, marks or body parts when they lack the vocabulary.

E  Why should words matter so much? Psychologists believe that humans, like many animals, are born with an 'approximate number sense'. Babies can tell a group of eight dots from a group of sixteen, but not eight from nine. Distinguishing exact numbers beyond about three appears to depend on language, which allows us to name a quantity and keep it in memory. Support comes from experiments in which English-speaking adults repeat a sentence aloud while trying to remember how many objects they have seen: their performance on exact tasks drops, while their approximate judgements are unaffected. Language, then, seems to act as a bridge between the vague sense we are born with and the precise arithmetic of schools and shops.

F  One finding in Marchetti's work argues strongly against the idea that the Ikuru are in any way limited. When a government school opened in a nearby town and Ikuru children began learning the national language, they mastered its number words within a few months, and adults who attended evening literacy classes did almost as well. The capacity had been present all along; what had been missing was a reason to use it. Marchetti draws a clear line: the lack of number words is a fact about a way of life, not about the minds of the people who live it.

G  Not all researchers accept this interpretation. Some argue that the tests were unfamiliar and artificial, and that Ikuru participants might have performed better had they been allowed to use gestures. Others point out that two or three words can still support surprisingly rich exchanges; the Ikuru manage barter with outsiders by pointing and displaying objects. There is also a practical urgency to the debate. As roads and mobile networks reach remote villages, communities adopt the number words of the trading language, often within a single generation. Linguists want to record such systems before they are replaced by borrowed ones. Once they disappear, the question of how number words arise may become impossible to study in living speakers.

passages.title: The Ground Beneath Our Feet
paras: A  Pick up a handful of healthy topsoil and you are holding one of the most complex habitats on the planet. A single teaspoon can contain billions of bacteria, several kilometres of fungal threads and thousands of tiny animals, from mites to microscopic worms. Most people think of soil as the inert stuff in which plants happen to stand. In reality it is a living system: its organisms break down dead material, release nutrients, bind particles into crumbs that hold water and air, and form partnerships with roots without which many crops would struggle to grow.

B  Soil is also painfully slow to make. Rock is broken down by frost, rain and the roots of pioneer plants, and the resulting mineral fragments are mixed with decaying leaves and animals by the organisms that feed on them. In temperate climates it can take several centuries to form a single centimetre. A farmer ploughing a field may therefore remove in a few seasons what nature took lifetimes to create. This mismatch of timescales is the root of the problem: because soil renews itself on a scale far beyond human planning, losses are for practical purposes permanent.

C  The most visible form of loss is erosion. When vegetation is stripped away, rain washes topsoil into rivers and wind lifts it into the air. The dust storms that swept across the American Great Plains in the 1930s, darkening skies as far away as the east coast, followed years of ploughing up native grassland, and drove hundreds of thousands of families from their farms. Erosion has since been joined by less dramatic threats. Heavy machinery compacts the ground until roots and earthworms cannot penetrate it; irrigation in dry regions draws salts to the surface, where they poison crops; and in growing cities, concrete and asphalt seal the earth so that it can no longer absorb rain or support life.

D  Perhaps the most worrying change is the least visible: the loss of organic matter. Soils store more carbon than the atmosphere and all vegetation combined, most of it in the dead plant material that gives healthy soil its dark colour. Repeated ploughing exposes this material to the air, allowing microbes to digest it and release carbon dioxide. The soil that results is paler, more compact and less able to retain water, so farmers compensate with fertiliser, which in turn alters the community of microbes. Estimates vary, but about a third of the world's farmland is judged to be moderately or severely degraded.

E  Evidence that the damage can be reversed comes from long-term trials. At Haverlow Research Farm, two neighbouring fields have been managed differently for thirty years. In one, wheat is grown year after year and the ground is ploughed every autumn. In the other, farmers plant a mixture of clover and rye after harvest, rotate their crops, and leave the stubble in place rather than turning it over. The second field now holds about a fifth more organic matter and absorbs rainfall roughly twice as fast. During the dry summer of 2018 it produced yields 15 per cent higher than the first, despite using a third less fertiliser.

F  Why, then, do not all farmers adopt such methods? Part of the answer is economic. The benefits build up over years, whereas the costs of new seed, new machinery and a possible dip in the first harvests fall at once. Tenant farmers on short leases have little incentive to improve land they may lose, and subsidies in many countries still reward volume rather than soil health. Part of the answer is knowledge: soil is hidden, and a farmer whose fields look green may not realise that their structure is failing until a drought or a storm exposes it.

G  Some governments are starting to respond. A few now pay farmers for measured increases in soil carbon, and several countries have begun mapping their soils in the same way that they survey roads or forests. Scientists, meanwhile, are developing cheap field tests that let a farmer count the earthworms in a spade-sized block of earth or measure how quickly water drains through it. Soil scientists warn that none of this will matter unless the public learns to value what lies underfoot. We have spent centuries learning to read the sky and the sea; the time has come, they say, to look down.
